newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals Whitewater ruling to Supreme Court.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals Whitewater ruling to Supreme Court.

text.p: The White House on Friday said it would appeal to the Supreme Court a ruling that ordered the release of notes taken by White House lawyers during conversations with first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit in St. Louis ruled that attorney-client privilege did not apply to the notes, which related to the long investigation into the Arkansas Whitewater financial affair by independent counsel Kenneth Starr. Starr had asked the notes be made available for a grand jury.

"The court's holding undercuts this president's, and all future presidents', ability to seek candid and confidential legal advice," White House legal counsel Charles Ruff said in announcing the decision to appeal to the high court.
He said he hoped to expedite the appeal through the court to allow it to act before the end of its term in late June.
The Clintons are not accused of any wrongdoing in the Whitewater affair, a complex web of Arkansas business deals, political contacts and allegations of coverup.

One set of notes was based on what Mrs. Clinton told White House lawyers about her grand jury testimony on Jan. 26, 1996 when she testified she did not know how a set of Whitewater-related legal billing records ended up in a library in the White House residence.

Another set of notes dated from July 11, 1995 and concerned Mrs. Clinton's activities in the days immediately following the July 1993 suicide of deputy White House legal counsel Vince Foster, who worked with Mrs. Clinton at the Rose Law Firm in Little Rock, Ark., when President Bill Clinton was governor of that state.
The notes were taken by Jane Sherburne and Miriam Nemetz, who were both lawyers with the White House legal counsel's office.
Ruff said in a statement that "until this ruling, the attorney-client privilege was universally assumed to apply to the work of private and government lawyers alike."
Starr, however, said he was pleased by the ruling.

"The court's decision reinforces a bedrock principle that we have been articulating for over two years in discussions with the White House: White House attorneys are government attorneys, not private attorneys."
The court said it reached its decision and filed it sealed on April 9 intending to release it later. In the interim, press reports disclosed some of the substance.

"We need not decide whether a governmental attorney-client privilege exists in other contexts, for it is enough to conclude that even if it does, the White House may not use the privilege to withhold potentially relevant information from a federal grand jury," the court said.

"The White House is correct ... in its assertion that the attorney-client privlege is the oldest known to the common law ... but the lengthy roots of the privilege do not necessarily mean that it must apply to this dispute within the federal government ...," the court said.
